passage:
Saturday
Today Francis and I went to see the dinosaur movie at the mall. Papa paid for the tickets and popcorn. After twenty minutes I was so bored. The dinosaurs only talked and talked. Francis whispered, "Let's go and play in the arcade." But I said no, because Papa had paid a lot of money, and if we left, the money would be wasted. So we sat for one and a half more hours. I nearly fell asleep. When we came out it was too late for the arcade. Papa asked if it was good. I said yes because he paid. He ruffled my hair and said, "That's my boy." My back hurts from sitting.
Samir

qa.q: What did Francis suggest after twenty minutes?
qa.a: Francis whispered, "Let's go and play in the arcade."

qa.q: Why did Samir stay for the whole movie even though he was bored?
qa.a: Papa had paid a lot, so leaving felt like wasting the money; Samir didn't see that the money was spent either way and only the time could still be saved.

qa.q: What could Samir think about the next time a paid-for thing turns boring?
qa.a: He could ask whether staying will make the next hour any better, since the money is already gone, and tell Papa honestly that it was boring.

qa.q: How might Francis feel about sitting through the movie?
qa.a: Francis probably felt bored and a bit disappointed about missing the arcade, after suggesting it so early.

grounding: Shows a boy sitting through a boring paid-for movie because leaving would feel like wasting the money.

passage: At the temple fair in their village near Madurai, Ramesh spent his whole ten rupees on a big, bright green sweet from a cart. One bite, and his face twisted. It tasted like soap and far too much sugar. His sister Aparna laughed. "Give it to the crows." "No! It cost ten rupees!" Ramesh took another bite, then another, chewing slowly with his eyes shut. His Ammamma, Rukmini, watched from the bangle stall. "Kanna, are you enjoying it?" she asked. "No," he said, taking another bite. "But I paid." By the time he finished, his stomach felt heavy, and he had no appetite for the hot bajji his Ammamma bought for everyone.

qa.q: How much did the green sweet cost?
qa.a: The sweet cost ten rupees.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh keep eating a sweet he disliked?
qa.a: Spending ten rupees made giving it away feel like losing the money, so he kept eating even though it tasted bad and made him feel heavy.

qa.q: What could Ammamma say to help Ramesh with this kind of choice?
qa.a: She could gently point out that the ten rupees are gone either way and eating more only adds a bad feeling, so next time he can stop and save room for something he likes.

qa.q: How might Aparna see her brother's choice?
qa.a: Aparna finds it funny and a little silly, since to her the obvious answer was to give the sweet to the crows.

grounding: Shows a boy eating a sweet he dislikes because he paid for it, even though finishing it spoils the rest of his evening.

passage: It was raining in Madrid, and Marek had been playing the same slow puzzle game on the family tablet for an hour. He had stopped enjoying it after ten minutes. The levels were all the same: push a box, push another box. His friend Santiago, who lived downstairs, knocked on the door holding a football. "Rain's stopped! Park?" Marek didn't look up. "I can't stop now. I've already played an hour. If I quit, it's all for nothing." Santiago waited, bouncing the ball, then shrugged and went down alone. Marek pushed another box. Then another. When he finally put the tablet down, it was dark and raining again.

qa.q: What was Santiago holding when he knocked on the door?
qa.a: Santiago was holding a football.

qa.q: Why did Marek feel he couldn't stop playing?
qa.a: Marek felt stuck, because he had already put in an hour and quitting felt like throwing that hour away. He kept going even though he was bored and the next hour would be just the same.

qa.q: What question could help Marek decide next time?
qa.a: He could ask, "If I were starting now, would I choose this game or the park?" The hour already spent can't come back either way.

qa.q: How might Santiago feel going down to the park alone?
qa.a: Santiago may feel disappointed and a bit confused, since the rain had stopped and Marek didn't even seem to be having fun.

grounding: Shows a boy continuing a boring game because he has already spent an hour on it, missing the chance to play outside.

passage: At the school canteen, Wasim, nine, bought a spicy paneer roll with his own twenty rupees. One bite and his eyes watered. He hated it. "Are you going to finish that?" asked Devika from his class, eating her plain idli. "I paid twenty rupees," Wasim said, and took another bite. His face turned red. He drank half his water bottle. He took another bite. "You don't even like it," Devika said. "But I paid." He chewed slowly, miserable, while the others ran out to play. By the last bite recess was almost over. Devika waited at the door. "You missed kho-kho," she said. Wasim wiped his eyes. "I didn't want to waste the money." "The money was already gone," Devika said. "You just wasted recess too."

qa.q: How much did Wasim pay for the paneer roll?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Wasim keep eating a roll he hated?
qa.a: He felt it would be a waste to stop because he had already paid, so he kept eating, miserable, even though the money was gone either way.

qa.q: What could Wasim do next time he buys something he doesn't like?
qa.a: He could stop after the first bites and ask himself what he wants to do now, like go and play, since eating more won't bring the twenty rupees back.

qa.q: How might Devika feel waiting at the door for Wasim?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit impatient and sorry for him, since he missed kho-kho for a roll he didn't even enjoy.

grounding: A boy keeps eating a spicy roll he hates because he paid for it, and misses recess games.

passage: I'm Leela. Last Sunday, visiting my friend Seema, I watched her son Tinku, ten, play a long property-trading board game with his cousins. The game had gone on for an hour and a half. The cousins had drifted off to the terrace. Tinku stayed, rolling for everyone, yawning. "Tinku, come play cricket," Seema called. "No, Mummy! I've been playing for ages. If I stop now, all that time is wasted." I can't say what he was thinking, but he kept going another half hour, sighing at every turn. By the time he packed it away, the cricket had ended. He sat on the steps, cross. Seema sat next to him and said softly, "The time was spent anyway, beta. The only question was what to do next."

qa.q: How long had the game gone on when the cousins gave up?
qa.a: The game had gone on for an hour and a half.

qa.q: Why might Tinku have kept playing a game he found boring?
qa.a: He seemed to feel that stopping would waste all the time already spent, so he kept going, bored and sighing, as if carrying on protected it.

qa.q: When Seema called him to cricket, what choice would have served Tinku better?
qa.a: He could have asked himself what he wanted to do now and gone to play cricket, since more board-game time wouldn't give back the hour and a half.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt watching Tinku sit alone with the game?
qa.a: Seema probably felt a mix of amusement and sympathy, and chose a gentle word afterward instead of a lecture.

grounding: A family friend watches a boy keep playing a boring board game alone because he has already spent so long on it.
